items.title: Bob Wilber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998
items.q: In 1950 George Wein started his first jazz venture which was to open up a club called Storyville, and I had such a big name in Boston he asked me to perform in the first band.

ctx.x: Yeah. I think the early years were so exciting with the recognition, with The Wildcats, and then I had my own band in Boston in 1947, ‘48, ‘49 at The Savoy Cafe, tremendously popular. It was at the beginning of the Dixieland Revival, and the great

interest among the college kids all over the East Coast in Dixieland music, and the place was jammed every night. In 1950 George Wein started his first jazz venture which was to open up a club called Storyville, and I had such a big name in Boston he asked me to perform in the first band. By then I’d relinquished the leadership of the band at The Savoy because I felt that they were in a rut and that they weren’t going anywhere, and I wanted to develop. So the band I bought in to Storyville was an entirely…
People kind of needed to have a compartment to put you in, in order to know how to listen to it.

items.title: George Wein — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He had Wilber and Sidney de Paris and Big Sid Catlett on the drums. And of course having Big Sid there was … that was a thrill. But I mean, that band cost me a thousand dollars a week.

ctx.x: Well, Mrs. Donnelley who owned the Club Sade [Mrs. Donahue owned the Savoy] and I knew the musicians and why not do that. And I did that successfully. That was a good thing for about a month or two, I don't know. I brought in Vic Dickenson and I brought in Wild Bill, I brought in Joe Thomas, a wonderful trumpet player, and with local musicians, and I was playing piano. We had some good weeks there. But I think when Phil Napoleon came in with his own band and sold Mrs. Donahue the idea of having his band – which…

night. One night – and Bob Wilber as the opener – and I asked Bob but he a different kind of band. He had Wilber and Sidney de Paris and Big Sid Catlett on the drums. And of course having Big Sid there was … that was a thrill. But I mean, that band cost me a thousand dollars a week. That's a lot of money. Six guys living in New York, paying their hotels … and getting a thousand dollars a week. Maybe it wasn't a thousand, maybe it was nine hundred. One night Louis Armstrong and the All-Stars were playing at…
[NOTE TO KIMERY re above and elsewhere– George refers to Pops as Louie, rather than Louis. Don't know if/how that should be handled. George does the same re Louie/Louis Lorillard.]
